The inconnu (Stenodus leucichthys) is a large salmonid native to Arctic and subarctic drainages of Eurasia and North America. Field surveys indicate females attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of 70 centimeters [Lp = 70 centimeters], a size threshold typically achieved after several years of growth in these cold, oligotrophic systems. The corresponding wet weight at puberty in females is approximately 3.13 kilograms [Wwp = approximately 3.13 kilograms], representing a substantial somatic investment before the onset of reproductive activity. Newly emerged alevins, transitioning from the yolk-sac stage, possess an extremely modest wet weight at birth of merely 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 2.5 millimeters and reflecting the high fecundity characteristic of the species. These endotrophic larvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the initial weeks post-hatching, gradually shifting to exogenous feeding as their yolk sacs are resorbed. The protracted larval and juvenile period in this species is an adaptation to the short, productive growing seasons of high-latitude environments, where maximising size prior to winter is crucial for overwinter survival.

At a constant water temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the maximum reproductive output of inconnu has been documented under controlled conditions that mimic their native thermal regime. Under this thermal regime, gravid females produce approximately 420,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 420,000 eggs per spawning event], and nearly all mature individuals spawn on an annual basis [F_R_i = spawn on an annual basis]. This annual reproductive cycle is typical of iteroparous salmonids inhabiting stable, cold environments where annual food availability is predictable but limited. The temperature of 11 °C represents an optimal thermal point for gametogenesis and embryonic development in this species, as it balances the metabolic demands of vitellogenesis against the energetic costs of physiological homeostasis. At temperatures significantly below this thermal optimum, egg production declines markedly and developmental rates slow considerably, restricting the species' southern distribution to deep, well-oxygenated lake systems that remain cool year-round. This thermal dependency underscores the vulnerability of inconnu populations to climate-driven warming in Arctic freshwaters.

The ultimate total length attained by inconnu, based on long-term mark-recapture studies in large river systems, reaches 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters]. This considerable maximum size positions the inconnu as one of the largest members of the subfamily Coregoninae, exceeding most whitefishes and ciscoes in asymptotic length. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of the species is substantial, estimated at 35.6 kilograms [Wwi = 35.6 kilograms] for the largest individuals. This asymptotic mass is derived from the length-weight relationship specific to the species, reflecting a deep, fusiform body shape that facilitates sustained swimming in river currents. The attainment of such a large body size is energetically demanding and requires multiple decades of growth, particularly given the low metabolic rates and short growing seasons characteristic of Arctic environments. Comparative analyses with other large-bodied salmonids suggest that this maximum size may ultimately be constrained by gill surface area limitations and the declining efficiency of oxygen uptake with increasing body mass, a physiological trade-off that sets an upper boundary on fish size in cold, oxygen-rich waters.

Longevity data for inconnu, gleaned from otolith annuli counts in populations from the Mackenzie River system, indicate a maximum lifespan of 22 years [am = 22 years] for individuals inhabiting waters at 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This lifespan, exceeding two decades, is typical of cold-water, slow-growing fishes that exhibit delayed maturity and iteroparous reproduction. The thermal regime of 11 °C appears to be especially conducive to prolonged survival, as metabolic wear-and-tear is reduced compared to warmer conditions that accelerate aging. Interestingly, the age at first reproduction does not occur until well after the onset of puberty; field observations show that most females do not spawn for the first time until approximately 8 years after hatching [tR = 8 years after hatching], a delay that allows for the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves to support the high fecundity observed at first breeding. This protracted juvenile phase is a common life-history strategy among long-lived Arctic fishes, balancing the benefits of early reproduction against the survival costs and reduced fecundity associated with smaller body sizes at younger ages.

Juvenile inconnu experience a period of rapid initial growth during their first few summers, exploiting the brief but intense pulse of zooplankton production in Arctic lakes and rivers. The post-larval transformation, marked by fin ray ossification and scale formation, occurs within the first growing season, after which the young-of-year fingerlings adopt a piscivorous diet. Sexual maturation is a gradual process, with gametogenesis onset triggered by a combination of photoperiod and achieving a threshold body condition. The wet weight at puberty, estimated at 3.13 kilograms [Wwp = 3.13 kilograms], is a critical energetic milestone that ensures females have sufficient lipid reserves to support the large clutch masses they produce. A comparison of the weight at puberty to the ultimate wet weight reveals that females invest heavily in somatic growth before initiating reproduction, as pubertal mass represents less than ten percent of the maximum achievable adult mass of 35.6 kilograms [Wwi = 35.6 kilograms]. This life-history pattern, characterised by delayed reproduction and extreme iteroparity, is well-suited to the stable but unproductive environments of Arctic freshwaters, where adult survival is high and interannual variability in recruitment is substantial.
